rationale: Start with a broad gradient to observe all 22 compounds and locate the elution window and critical pairs. A moderate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Shorten the gradient to target a last peak within 10 minutes while isolating the effect of slope. Comparing the critical-pair patterns will identify which separations need temperature or solvent-window changes rather than a longer gradient.

The late near-coelution barely improved with a shallower gradient, making temperature the next selectivity lever. Keep the gradient unchanged and test 60 C to separate temperature effects while preserving a short run.

Lower temperature should improve the early critical separation, which deteriorated at 60 C. A 12-minute gradient should also strengthen slope-sensitive middle pairs while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction and narrow the gradient window to spend more time separating the middle and late clusters without extending the last retention time. This also tests whether changing the window can improve the persistent late near-coelution.

Further narrow and shift the gradient window to improve the remaining slope-sensitive pairs while targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. The first peak is still retained at phi0 0.15, so this run will also establish how much starting-strength increase the early peaks tolerate.

Back off the starting strength one step to recover separation in the early and middle clusters while retaining a narrow gradient window. The current 0.45-minute time margin should accommodate this change with little or no time penalty.

Test temperature selectivity in the improved solvent window, where the early critical pair now has resolution to spare. Holding the gradient fixed will show whether warming can improve the late cluster without sacrificing the middle pairs.

Return to 25 C and test a narrower, shallower gradient shifted toward the late cluster. This probes whether late-pair gains can outweigh possible compression or reordering among the early peaks while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Use the time margin from injection 6 for a slightly shallower gradient, targeting the middle and late unresolved pairs. The predicted last peak is near 10 minutes, and the early pair had sufficient resolution at this starting composition.

Test a lower final organic fraction so the late cluster transitions into an isocratic hold, providing a different selectivity regime for the persistent near-coelution. The faster initial gradient limits the time cost of the lower-strength hold.

Refine around the best method with a slightly lower starting fraction and a slope chosen to keep the last peak near 10 minutes. This should strengthen the marginal middle separation while preserving the favorable low-temperature selectivity.

Move the late cluster decisively into the final hold to test selectivity outside the gradient regime, since slope and temperature changes have barely separated its closest pair. A short gradient and lower starting fraction aim to limit the time cost and preserve early retention.

Probe a substantially shallower gradient at higher starting strength to see whether reordered early peaks and improved late separation offer a better region. This is an exploratory run; injection 7 remains the benchmark.

Combine a slightly shallower gradient than the best run with modest warming to offset added retention time. This tests whether slope gains in the middle and late clusters outweigh the smaller temperature-related selectivity losses.

Test the smallest temperature increase from injection 10 to bring its last peak below 10 minutes. Holding the gradient fixed will determine whether removing the time penalty compensates for the selectivity change.
Test a slope between injections 6 and 10, retaining low-temperature selectivity while avoiding injection 10’s time penalty. The final composition should still place the last peak inside the gradient.

Test a lower starting fraction with a slightly steeper gradient than injection 7, aiming to preserve middle-pair resolution while finishing below 10 minutes. This refines the promising low-temperature region without relying on a late hold.

Explore beyond the early-pair crossing seen at higher starting strength, using a much shallower gradient to improve the late cluster. This tests a distinct selectivity region before spending the remaining injections on final refinement.

Return to the strongest region with a slope close to injection 10, but end the gradient before the last peaks elute. This tests whether a brief final hold can improve late selectivity enough to offset any added retention time.

Refine temperature immediately around the best method, using a single 5 C increase rather than the larger shifts tested previously. This checks for a favorable local selectivity change while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test a slightly shallower gradient with moderate warming to bring the predicted last peak close to 10 minutes. This checks whether improved middle-pair separation can outweigh the temperature-related losses observed at steeper slopes.

Refine the lower-starting-strength region with a slope between injections 12 and 18. This targets full credit for the middle pairs while keeping the last peak close to the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to strengthen its marginal middle and late separations. The predicted last peak is just above 10 minutes, so this checks whether the resolution gain outweighs the small time penalty.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower slope than injection 10 at the favorable low temperature. This targets its marginal middle separation and late cluster, accepting a possible small time penalty if the resolution gain compensates.
